column1: # ---- 04-compliance/T5 ----
No tier ships without its gap measured against Tier 1, and T5 is the procedure that produces that measurement and the release gate that enforces it.
Tier 1 must exist even though it may never run in production, because without an oracle there is no gap and without a gap there is no engineering, only hope.
The Tier-k-to-Tier-1 gap answers how much the fast path costs, and the fix lives in the tier itself.
The Tier-1-to-perfect-foresight distance answers whether the optimiser is weak versus the world being uncertain, and the fix lives in either the scenario model or the Planner.
Solve time and objective as functions of scenario count and breakpoint count answer whether the configured knobs sit at the right point on the accuracy/speed curve.
Tier 1 is the joint stochastic MILP with reserve capacities as decision variables alongside spot dispatch and the coupling constraints explicit.
Tier 1 is the accuracy reference, does not need to be fast, and runs offline on every backtest day regardless of which tier ships.
The oracle run requires Tier 1 to reach Optimal or GapLimited status with a MIP gap at or below the oracle gap tolerance, defaulting to 1e-4.
The oracle records the objective, trajectory, reserve volumes, MIP gap, solve time and status per tick.
Every tier is solved on the identical recorded C2 bundle and StateSnapshot, because anything else measures input differences rather than tier differences.
The oracle budget is generous but bounded and recorded, because an oracle that timed out at a 3 per cent gap is not an oracle and the recorded MIP gap is part of the gap arithmetic.
Rounding to tick and lot sizes happens only at C3, because rounding earlier corrupts the optimality-gap measurement, and it is this measurement that the rounding rule protects.
The oracle runs under the reproducibility manifest, because a non-reproducible oracle makes every gap unfalsifiable.

Ticks where Tier 1 fails to reach the oracle gap tolerance are reported separately and never dropped, because silently dropping the hard instances biases every reported gap downward and the hard instances are the ones that matter.
The absolute gap is the oracle objective minus the tier objective, in EUR.
The relative gap is the absolute gap divided by the larger of the oracle objective's magnitude and a configured EUR floor.
Without a denominator floor, a tick whose oracle objective is near zero produces an unbounded relative gap and poisons every percentile.
The absolute gap in EUR is the one that gates, because a 40 per cent relative gap on a EUR 3 tick is noise while a 2 per cent relative gap on a peak-critical day is not.
A negative gap — the tier beating the oracle — is possible only through an oracle gap tolerance or a defect, and is reported as a finding rather than truncated to zero.
The gap is reported as p50, p90, p99 and worst case, never as a mean, because the tail is where a fast heuristic destroys value.
The gap distribution of a heuristic is sharply right-skewed: near zero on the many days when nothing is binding and large on the few days when reserve, peak and spot compete for the same headroom.
A mean gap is dominated by the uninteresting mass: ninety ordinary days at EUR 0.40 and ten critical days at EUR 300 give a mean of EUR 30.36, which describes no actual day and hides the EUR 300.
A mean gap is not robust, because one oracle timeout, one negative gap or one outlier day moves it, while percentiles do not move.
A mean gap answers the wrong question, because what is needed is the cost on the day it goes wrong.
A heuristic that is fine on average and terrible on the ten days that matter is worse than not having the tier at all, because it has been trusted.
The gap report carries p50, p90, p99 and worst in EUR and per cent, the count of ticks in the tail above a configured EUR threshold, the cumulative gap over the corpus, and the negative-gap count.
The cumulative gap over the corpus is the only meaningful aggregate, because it is a sum and not an average.
The worst case is always named with its day, tick, regime and what was binding, plus a link to the recorded seam.
An unnamed worst case is a number nobody can act on, while a named one is a fixture and usually a bug report.
The gap regimes are declared, derived from recorded data rather than from the tier's own output, and every one is reported with the full percentile set.

High-spread days are those whose intraday max-minus-min of the ensemble-mean day-ahead price exceeds the corpus 90th percentile, and are separated because the arbitrage term is large there and a mis-priced headroom transfer costs most.

Peak-critical days are those with peakCritical set or the modelled POI trajectory within a configured margin of the realised peak, and are separated because a heuristic that trades a peak breach for a spread is catastrophic there and invisible on average.

High reserve price days are those whose block-mean aFRR capacity price exceeds the corpus 90th percentile, and are separated because the reservation price matters most there and Tier 3's learned surface is most likely out of distribution.

Qualification-critical days are those with qualCritical set, and are separated because losing a year of network-charge reduction for a day's spread is the single largest downside event in the business case.

Negative-price episodes are days with any slot whose ensemble-mean day-ahead price is below zero, and are separated because the simultaneity invariant becomes non-redundant there and the LP relaxation can misbehave.
High activation days are those whose realised activation fraction exceeds the 90th percentile, and are separated for commitment feasibility under stress.
DST transition days are taken from the calendar and are separated because calendar-driven formulation errors surface as a gap.
Degraded-mode days are any ticks not in NORMAL, and are separated because a gap under a widened risk profile is a different measurement.
A tier passes only if it passes per regime rather than merely in aggregate.
Because ICoOptimizer escalates at runtime, the shipped gap is not Tier 3's gap but the gap of the escalation policy.
The pure Tier 3 gap with escalation disabled measures the learned surface itself.
The Tier 2 gap on every tick measures the escalation target's quality.
The shipped gap under the escalation policy as configured is the number that gates the release.
The escalation rate is reported by trigger and by regime.
A configuration that escalates on 60 per cent of ticks is a Tier 2 deployment with extra steps and its latency budget should be assessed as such.
The true gap lies within the measured gap plus or minus the oracle's own absolute MIP gap, and the gap is reported with that oracle-gap band attached.
The oracle's own MIP gap must be much smaller than the median tier gap, or the oracle cannot resolve the quantity being measured.

If the oracle's own MIP gap is comparable to the tier gap being measured the measurement is not meaningful and the report says so rather than printing a number, and the remedy is tightening the oracle tolerance or shrinking the instance.

T5 asserts that the gap it measures and the settlement optimalityGap bucket agree over the same period within tolerance, and a divergence means the counterfactual re-run and the oracle run are not using the same inputs.
The perfect-foresight bound solves the same day with the realised path known as a single deterministic scenario, all other inputs identical.

The perfect-foresight run keeps the same feasible set: physical bounds, POI envelope, commitments and regulatory constraints are identical, because perfect foresight removes uncertainty rather than physics.
A perfect-foresight run that also relaxes a bound measures nothing.

The perfect-foresight run keeps the same market mechanics: gate structure and non-anticipativity across market stages remain, so it knows the future but the DA gate still closes before the intraday window.
Removing the market staging from the perfect-foresight run turns the bound into a fantasy and inflates the reported uncertainty cost.
Confirmed commitments still bind in the perfect-foresight run, because the ledger is history rather than a decision.
Perfect foresight is a bound and not a target, and no configuration change should ever be justified by closing the gap to it.
The distance from Tier 1 to perfect foresight is the irreducible loss under the current information set, whose fix lives in Belief, the scenario model and the data sources.
The distance from the shipped tier to Tier 1 is reducible by better optimisation, whose fix lives in the tier ladder.

A large Tier1-to-PF distance with a small tier-to-Tier-1 gap means the optimiser is close to the best achievable under uncertainty and the loss is informational, so optimisation work has almost no headroom.

A small Tier1-to-PF distance with a large tier-to-Tier-1 gap means the problem is nearly deterministic and the heuristic is leaving money on the table, so the escalation thresholds or the learned surface need work.
Both distances large means two independent problems that must be addressed separately rather than letting one hide behind the other.
Both distances small means the system is near its ceiling on this corpus and the search should be for a missing lever.

Self-consumption is not a missing lever, because it is priced through the delineation accumulators, and a plan that over-consumes behind the meter shows up as a λ_11 misprice rather than as a missing view.
Without the headroom decomposition a team spends quarters improving an optimiser whose remaining gap is entirely forecast uncertainty, or tuning forecasts to close a gap that is pure heuristic loss.
The perfect-foresight bound costs one extra Tier 1 solve per day and it settles the argument.
The perfect-foresight distance is reported with the same percentile discipline as the gap — p50, p90, p99 and worst, per regime — and the headroom split ratio is reported per regime.
Tier 2's Lagrangian decomposition gives, at any iteration, a bound on the true optimum, so the gap to the best primal solution is a number that can be reported rather than a hope.
Unlike the Tier-1 gap, the Tier 2 certificate is available per solve, at runtime, in production, with no oracle present.
A Tier 2 result carries the feasible primal objective, the Lagrangian dual bound, the certified gap and relative gap, the iteration count, the exit reason and the reservation prices.
A Tier 2 exit reason is one of Converged, IterationCap, TimeCap or NumericalTrouble.

Every Tier 2 solve asserts the certified gap is non-negative within tolerance, the primal is feasible on every exit path including TimeCap, the dual bound is finite, and the reservation prices are finite and non-negative.
A non-converged Tier 2 exit reason is recorded in PlanResult and in the settlement record.

A dual bound that dips below the primal is a broken relaxation — a coupling constraint relaxed with the wrong sign, or a subproblem solved to the wrong sense — and it invalidates every bound the tier has ever reported, so it is a HALT.
The certified relative gap distribution is reported as p50, p90, p99 and worst per regime, gated on p99 within the configured band.
The Tier 2 exit-reason mix is reported and a rising NumericalTrouble rate blocks release.
The distribution of iterations to converge, and its dependence on instance size, feeds the latency evidence for the deferred latency budget.
On the oracle corpus the certified gap must dominate the measured Tier-1-minus-Tier-2 gap within tolerance, because a certificate that under-states the true gap is worse than no certificate.
The reservation prices are compared against the spot opportunity cost they are supposed to equal and reviewed by a human, because they are diagnostically valuable precisely for being human-checkable.
Tier 2's central claim is that the reservation price is provably consistent with spot opportunity cost rather than a heuristic weighting.
A reservation price of EUR 400/MW/h on a flat, low-price day contradicts the consistency claim and points at the subgradient step-size rule or a mis-scaled coupling row.
The scenario-count sweep covers S in 1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256, recording objective, solve time, row and column counts, binary count and MIP gap per tier.
The breakpoint sweep covers 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 breakpoints per curve, recording objective, solve time, binary count and approximation error against the finest grid.
The reference values are the objective at S = 256 and at the finest breakpoint grid.
The objective-versus-S curve shows where the accuracy curve flattens, and scenario count is a first-class tuning parameter with a measurable cost/quality curve.
The solve-time-versus-S curve reports p50 and p99 per tier and is the cost side of the scenario-count trade.
The reduction fidelity curve reports the marginal-mean error and a Wasserstein distance to the full ensemble against S, distinguishing more-scenarios-help from the reduction being bad at small S.
The objective-versus-breakpoint-count curve reports objective and approximation error, because breakpoint count is a tuning knob with a measurable accuracy/speed trade-off.
The solve-time-versus-breakpoint-count curve reports p50, p99 and binary count, which is where the cost of a General-curvature PWL becomes visible.
The solve-time-versus-binary-count scatter is coloured by the per-term binary attribution and is the attribution instrument plotted.
The solve-time-versus-row-and-column-count scatter detects super-linear blow-up before it reaches production.
The determinism-cost curve compares reproducibility and production configuration solve times, making the cost of determinism a number rather than an argument.
The configured scenario count and breakpoint count must sit at a declared point on the curve, with the declaration recorded in the configuration next to the value.
A configuration value with no T5 citation next to it is a guess, and the release checklist flags it.
T5 is a release gate rather than a merge gate, and runs pre-release overnight on a holdout corpus that is not the corpus any tier was tuned on.
The gate requires the Tier 1 oracle run to have completed over the whole holdout corpus, with the count and identity of ticks failing the oracle tolerance reported rather than dropped.
The gate requires every tier that can run in production to have its gap measured, including tiers reachable only by escalation.
The gate requires the shipped gap reported as p50, p90, p99 and worst, in EUR and per cent, per regime.
The gate requires per-regime p99 within the configured band and the worst case named with its recorded seam.
The gate assesses peak-critical and qualification-critical regimes against their own tighter band, because a heuristic that is fine on average and terrible on the ten days that matter does not ship.
The gate requires the perfect-foresight bound computed with the Tier1-to-PF distance and the headroom split reported per regime.
The gate requires Tier 2 dual-bound certification with no invalid bound anywhere in the corpus, every exit path returning a feasible primal, and the exit-reason mix within band.
The gate requires the scaling curves regenerated and the configured values cited against the current curves.
The gate requires solve-time p99 per tier and per gate type recorded, feeding the deferred latency budget decision.
The gate requires no configuration value in the shipped config to lack a T5 citation.
A tier whose gap exceeds its band in any regime does not ship as the production path, though it may still ship as an escalation target if its gap is acceptable there.
If the oracle could not resolve the gap the measurement is void, and the remedy is to tighten the oracle or reduce the instance rather than ship on an unresolved gap.
An invalid Tier 2 dual bound is a stop-ship, because the bound is the product.
A regression against the previous release's gap distribution blocks release unless accompanied by a stated, accepted trade such as a latency improvement with a quantified gap cost.
If the scaling curves show the configured scenario count past the knee, the configuration is re-declared or the citation updated.
The gate does not require the gap to be small but requires it to be measured, named, conditioned and accepted.

A tier with a p99 gap of EUR 200 on peak-critical days may be perfectly acceptable if the latency it buys is necessary and the escalation policy covers those days, but that has to be a decision someone took with the number in front of them.
